evidence.label: A continuum temperature singularity for a radial pair potential
A radial continuum phase transition with algebraic decay

headline: Two built pair potentials give particles in space a first-order phase transition across a range of densities.
scope: It covers single-species particles in three dimensions with engineered radial pair potentials. It says nothing about Lennard-Jones or real fluids.
plain: A phase transition, like water boiling, shows up as a sudden jump in energy at one temperature. The papers build two simple distance-based force rules between identical particles in space that produce such a jump. The same critical temperature works over a whole range of densities. One rule is bounded everywhere and its pull fades at a fixed power rate.
doesNot: This does not show a phase transition for the Lennard-Jones potential or any real substance.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It gives single-species radial pair potentials with a proved temperature jump, one with a power-law tail.

explanation:
Heat a pot of water at sea level. At 100 °C the temperature stops rising for a while. The added heat goes into turning liquid into steam. The energy of the water jumps while the temperature stays put. Physicists call this a first-order phase transition.

Mathematicians want to prove such a jump from first principles. Start with many identical particles in space. Each pair of particles has an energy that depends only on their distance r. That rule is called a radial pair potential, φ(r). The free energy is a number that sums up how the whole system behaves at a given temperature and density. Density is the number of particles per unit volume. A jump in its slope with respect to inverse temperature, written β, is the sign of a transition. The slope here is the average energy, so a jump means the energy leaps at one temperature, like the boiling water.

Can one simple pair rule produce such a jump for particles moving freely in space[1]? Barry Simon highlighted this question in his list of problems in mathematical physics[16]. Earlier proofs needed extra structure. Ruelle used two kinds of particles[7]. Lebowitz, Mazel and Presutti added a repulsive four-body force on top of pair forces[8]. A recent model by He, Jauslin, Lebowitz and Peled depends on a fixed grid of cubes[17].

The tail of the potential matters. The total pull from far-away particles adds up like the sum of r² × φ(r) over distances. If φ(r) falls like 1/r³, that sum from 1 to R equals the natural log of R. At R = 1,000 it is about 6.9, and at R = 10^12 about 27.6. It keeps growing without end. If φ(r) falls like r^(−3−1/32), the same sum stays below 32. It is about 6.2 at R = 1,000 and about 18.5 at R = 10^12.

The first paper builds a stable radial pair potential in three dimensions[2]. Stable means the total energy is never lower than a fixed constant times the number of particles. The potential blows up at very short range, attracts at a middle range, and has a tail that fades faster than 1/r³[3]. Its free energy has a slope jump at one inverse temperature. That one temperature works for every density in an open interval[2]. The paper does not prove that the tail fades faster by any fixed power[4].

The second paper builds a different potential that stays bounded and continuous everywhere[12]. Its tail is at most a constant times r^(−3−1/32), so the far-field sum above stays finite. It again has a slope jump at one common inverse temperature across a range of densities[13].

The obstacle is that a jump in density alone is not enough[9]. The proof needs two different energies at the same density and the same temperature. The usual tool lets the attraction's range go to infinity. But the jump must belong to one fixed potential, not a limit[14]. And smoothing an approximation can erase a corner[11]. The first paper uses a geometric fact. At most four particles can all be within one tiny range of distances from each other in space[10]. Four such points form a nearly regular tetrahedron, and a fifth cannot fit. This keeps the energy under control. In the second paper, the fixed power bound limits how strong each far attraction can be[15].

These are built potentials, not real ones. The first paper makes no claim about the standard Lennard-Jones potential used for real gases[5]. It does not identify the phases as liquid, gas or solid[6].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal versions of both main theorems. They cover the core potential with its fast-fading tail, and the bounded potential with the r^(−3−1/32) bound. Each has a slope jump at one inverse temperature across an open density interval. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proofs hold. Lean has formal versions of both theorems; no specialist review is published, and the potentials are engineered rather than physical.

claims.text: The problem asks whether a single species with a stable radial pair potential has a temperature singularity.
claims.sourceQuote: We consider an existence problem: can a single species of particles in $\R^3$, interacting through a stable radial pair potential, have a temperature singularity at one fixed density, and can the same critical inverse temperature work throughout an open interval of densities?

claims.text: The canonical free energy has a strict downward derivative jump at one common inverse temperature throughout an open density interval.
claims.sourceLine: free energy has a strict downward derivative jump at one common finite positive
claims.sourceQuote: We construct a stable radial pair potential in three dimensions whose canonical free energy has a strict downward derivative jump at one common finite positive inverse temperature throughout an open interval of positive densities.

claims.sourceLine: The potential has a divergent repulsive core, a nontrivial attractive interval,
claims.sourceQuote: The potential has a divergent repulsive core, a nontrivial attractive interval, and an integrable tail satisfying $\phi(r)=o(r^{-3})$.
